posts.content:
Raspberries are at their juiciest in August, and so is our round-up this month. From Shenzhen to South Wales, here's everything the Raspberry Pi team and our partners have been up to.

We're currently in Shenzhen, China, for IOTE 2026, where you can find us exhibiting alongside EDATEC-Industrial Raspberry Pi and showcasing our technology in action, including Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5. Speaking of which, provisioning Compute Module 5 just got a whole lot easier: the new Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 Programming Jig lets you program Compute Module 5 with an operating system and security configuration with a single clamp of its lever.

On the AI side, our friends at Google showed you how to get LiteRT running on Raspberry Pi for high-performance, on-device inference, and shared a deep dive into pairing LiteRT with Gemma models for real-time edge AI applications. Our latest podcast episode explored how Raspberry Pi is quietly powering AI at the edge, from counting sheep in fields to spotting hi-vis jackets on construction sites. And we're looking forward to Drone X  in London this September, where we'll be back exhibiting for another year.

In partner news, Candera's free CGI Studio Community Edition is now available to download, giving makers, students, and small teams access to professional HMI design at no cost. And a huge well done to the team at Sony - UK Technology Centre, who walked 50km along the Wales Coast Path this month in aid of Macmillan Cancer Support.

posts.content:
Ever wondered what it actually takes to work out the carbon footprint of a circuit board? There's no meter for that.

We break every product down to its bill of materials: every PCB, capacitor and connector weighed and mapped against the ecoinvent database. Then we work with LCA specialists to build a bottom-up picture of embodied carbon, from raw materials to manufacturing and distribution.

It's painstaking work, but it means our Scope 3 numbers are grounded in real data, not industry averages, and it shows us exactly where to focus to build greener products.

Read the full story on how we measure what's inside: 
 https://lnkd.in/emKadBma

repost.content:
Today, we're kicking off the first phase of the research preview for Model Hardware Standard (MHS): a new standard for AI agents to safely operate physical equipment in scientific research and advanced manufacturing. 

Connecting AI to hardware today means weeks of bespoke integration per device, with no standard way for agents to operate equipment safely. MHS cuts integration to hours or minutes, while providing an interface that makes devices discoverable and enables agents to operate them within their safety limits.

In early testing, AI agents used MHS to:

- Run a drug-discovery experiment with real-time error handling at Genentech
- Compress an imaging experiment from weeks to a single day at HHMI Janelia Research Campus
- Improve laser stabilization on QuEra's quantum computers from 58% to 99.3%.

There’s more to learn before we open source MHS. LLMs still lack physical intuition, having learned about the physical world from text and images. The research preview will let us build more safety evaluations and strengthen protections for the use of AI in the physical world. 

MHS started during a collaboration between Anthropic’s beneficial deployments team and Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) Janelia Research Campus. The collaboration has since grown to include partners across science, robotics, and manufacturing.

We're inviting stakeholders across science and industry to join the research preview and help shape the standard. 

We look forward to moving MHS forward with our industry partners and, soon, the open-source community.

posts.content:
Our July edition is live. Between the heatwaves and the odd thunderstorm, it’s been a properly eventful month. Plenty has been happening across the Raspberry Pi ecosystem, too — and we’ve got the round-up to prove it.

This month, we went three inches bigger with the launch of the 10" Raspberry Pi Touch Display 2, available now at $80. We also published a new white paper on the industry-wide shift fromMLC to TLC flash memory and how it’s affecting our Compute Modules, including a clear explanation of what it means for reliability, endurance, and existing designs (short version: no code changes needed, and we've got you covered).

On the software side, Candera launched a free Community Edition of its CGI Studio HMI design tool for Raspberry Pi 4 and 5, opening up professional-grade interface design to makers and small teams at no cost. Our friends at Intel and Ultralytics showed you how to deploy YOLO computer vision models on Raspberry Pi using OpenVINO, and we took a look at how to use OpenClaw to turn your Raspberry Pi into a safely contained autonomous assistant.

And in our latest Powered by Raspberry Pi round-up: vivariums, drone light shows, and a TV kit for snooker players — proof that our little computers keep turning up in the most unexpected places.

🚀 Raspberry Pi Pico 2 and Pico 2 W is now supported in .NET nanoFramework!

The latest Raspberry Pi microcontroller board combines the new RP2350 running at up to 150 MHz, 520 KB SRAM, integrated Wi‑Fi and Bluetooth, enhanced security features, and the unique ability to support both Arm Cortex‑M33 and RISC‑V architectures.

With .NET nanoFramework, you can now bring modern C# development to this powerful board, benefiting from Visual Studio debugging, managed code, and access to the rich nanoFramework ecosystem. Both the RP2350 and RP2350 Wi-Fi are now supported.

✅ Wi‑Fi support (RP2350 W)
✅ GPIO, I2C, SPI, PWM, UART and ADC support
✅ Visual Studio debugging with breakpoints
✅ Hundreds of device bindings from nanoFramework.IoT.Device
✅ Familiar C# development experience on a microcontroller

The Pico ecosystem is already hugely popular, and support for the Pico 2 W opens the door for even more connected IoT projects built with .NET nanoFramework.

And something important: this reinforces the excellent partnership with ChibiOS which also powers this device! ChibiOS has been our RTOS of choice for all the Raspberry Pi Pico family.

posts.content:
I've been a Raspberry Pi fan for years. So when I found myself at embedded world Exhibition&Conference in March, running the Screenly stand inside the Raspberry Pi Partners booth, it already felt like a privilege. Thanks to the Screenly team and Viktor Petersson for the opportunity.

Then I got to spend time with the Raspberry Pi team and engineers in person. People whose work I'd followed for years. The conversations were genuine, and honestly, the whole thing felt a little unreal. One of those moments you don't fully appreciate until it's over.

And then, somewhere between those conversations, I got hands-on with the Sharp MPi5 Kit.

Raspberry Pi CM5, slotted directly into the display using the Intel SDM standard. No external player. No extra box. The computer lives inside the screen and powers up from it. It's a surprisingly small and clean piece of hardware.

I got to load Screenly OS on it right there at the event. When I ran into an issue, I just walked over to the Raspberry Pi booth and talked directly with the engineer who worked on it. As someone who loves making things and digging into hardware, I found that moment to be something else. Being able to go straight to the source like that is not something you get every day.

And now: Screenly ships preloaded on it. Plug in, register, publish. That's it. 

But beyond the hardware, what stays with me most is the people. So many faces I had only ever seen on a screen, a forum post, a GitHub profile, a comment thread. Finally meeting them in person, in the same room, was worth the trip alone.

Months later, I'm still glad I was in that room 🤗

#RaspberryPi #DigitalSignage #Screenly #EW26

Our June edition is live. We've had a heatwave, a downpour, and England fans convincing themselves that this is finally the year it’s coming home… On the whole, a perfectly normal start to a British summer.

With the EU Cyber Resilience Act deadline moving ever closer, we know it's front of mind for many of our customers. To help provide some clarity, we’ve put together a brief overview of where things stand and what they might mean for integrators’ Raspberry Pi–based products (the short version: we're on it).

Also this month: 
Hellbender Inc. launched Tendryl, a monocular camera powered by Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 and a Hailo-8 AI accelerator, built for those ready to take their Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ applications into production. NoviSign Digital Signage announced support for Raspberry Pi devices in its digital signage software, giving organisations a flexible new option for their signage deployments. The latest episode of the Raspberry Pi Podcast asked whether a Raspberry Pi can replace your desktop PC at home or in the office. One maker built a remarkable LiDAR scanner that took our YouTube channel by storm, while another designed a custom film scanner using a Raspberry Pi 5 and a projector from 1928 to digitise his father's high school footage.

Imagine being three years old and struggling to hear your teacher, your parents, your friends.

Glue ear is one of the most common causes of hearing loss in young children, and for many it goes unnoticed at exactly the age when listening and language matter most.

Dr Tamsin H. Brown has dedicated her career to changing that. As a paediatrician and co-founder of Hear Glue Ear, she has been working with Raspberry Pi to develop bone conduction headphones that are simple enough for a child to use and affordable enough to reach the children who need them most.

She recently sat down with Cambridgeshire Deaf Association to talk about her work and why she cares so deeply about it. Skip to 12:45 for the Raspberry Pi bit 👇

https://lnkd.in/e_MaTTap

The headphones are available in the UK from The Pi Hut: https://lnkd.in/e2tDA4rv
